content:
# Disagreement Log — 1 Clement Chapter 5

**Date:** 2026-03-17
**Agents:** EMET (literal) | LOGOS (formal) | PNEUMA (dynamic)
**Total Disagreements:** 15

---

## Disagreement 1 — 5:1 "champions of the most recent times" vs. "athletes who were nearest to our own day" vs. "champions who lived in our own recent times"

- **EMET:** "champions of the most recent times"
- **LOGOS:** "athletes who were nearest to our own day"
- **PNEUMA:** "champions who lived in our own recent times"
- **Greek:** *tous eggista genomenous athlētas* — the athletes who became/lived nearest (to us)
- **Ruling:** SOPHIA uses "athletes of most recent times." *Athlētēs* = athlete/contestant; both "champions" and "athletes" work; SOPHIA prefers "athletes" as more literal to the athletic-contest metaphor Clement employs throughout.

---

## Disagreement 2 — 5:2 "pillars" — all agree, no disagreement

- All three agents use "pillars." Recorded for completeness.
- **Note:** *stulos* = pillar; the same word Paul uses for James, Peter, and John in Gal 2:9.

---

## Disagreement 3 — 5:2 "persecuted and contended" vs. "persecuted and fought" vs. "persecuted and fought"

- **EMET:** "persecuted and contended unto death"
- **LOGOS:** "persecuted and contended to the death"
- **PNEUMA:** "persecuted and fought to the death"
- **Greek:** *ediōchthēsan kai emachesanto mechri thanatou* — were persecuted and struggled/fought unto death
- **Ruling:** SOPHIA uses "persecuted and contended to the death" (LOGOS). "Contended" preserves the athletic contest imagery.

---

## Disagreement 4 — 5:4 "labors" vs. "trials" vs. "hardships"

- **EMET:** "many labors"
- **LOGOS:** "many trials"
- **PNEUMA:** "countless hardships"
- **Greek:** *pollous ponous* — many toils/labors/sufferings
- **Ruling:** SOPHIA uses "many labors." *Ponos* = labor/toil/suffering; "labors" fits the athletic imagery. "Countless" (PNEUMA) overstates *pollous* (many).

---

## Disagreement 5 — 5:4 "gave his testimony" vs. "borne his witness" vs. "given his testimony"

- **EMET:** "having given his testimony"
- **LOGOS:** "having borne his witness"
- **PNEUMA:** "having given his testimony"
- **Greek:** *martyrēsas* — having witnessed/testified (martyrdom root)
- **Ruling:** SOPHIA uses "having given his testimony." This is the earliest technical use of the martyr-vocabulary. Both renderings preserve the root; "testimony" is slightly more widely understood.

---

## Disagreement 6 — 5:4 "glorious place" vs. "place of glory" — word order

- **EMET:** "went to the glorious place which was his due"
- **LOGOS:** "went to the place of glory that was his due"
- **PNEUMA:** "went to the place of glory he deserved"
- **Greek:** *eis ton opheilomenon tēs doxēs topon* — to the owed/due place of glory
- **Ruling:** SOPHIA uses "went to the place of glory that was his due" (LOGOS). "Owed/due" should be preserved; Peter's glory was earned.

---

## Disagreement 7 — 5:5 "showed the way to the prize" vs. "demonstrated the prize" vs. "showed him the path to the prize"

- **EMET:** "Paul showed the way to the prize of patient endurance"
- **LOGOS:** "Paul demonstrated the prize of endurance"
- **PNEUMA:** "jealousy and contention showed him the path to the prize"
- **Greek:** *ton brabeion tēs hupomonēs edelōsen* — he pointed out / made evident the prize of endurance
- **Ruling:** SOPHIA uses "Paul demonstrated the prize of patient endurance." Paul's suffering *demonstrated* (made visible) what endurance wins. PNEUMA reverses the subject.

---

## Disagreement 8 — 5:6 "exiled" vs. "exiled" — all agree

- All agents agree on "exiled." Recorded. *phugadeuō* = to banish/exile.

---

## Disagreement 9 — 5:6 "bore chains" vs. "bore chains" — all agree on content, PNEUMA restructures

- **EMET/LOGOS:** "Seven times he bore chains"
- **PNEUMA:** "Seven times he was put in chains"
- **Ruling:** SOPHIA uses "Seven times he bore chains." The active bearing of chains honors Paul's endurance; passive "was put in chains" diminishes agency.

---

## Disagreement 10 — 5:6 "herald" — all agree

- All three agents use "herald" for *kērux*. Recorded for completeness.

---

## Disagreement 11 — 5:6 "noble renown" vs. "noble fame" vs. "lasting glory"

- **EMET:** "won noble renown for his faith"
- **LOGOS:** "attained noble fame through his faith"
- **PNEUMA:** "won lasting glory through his faith"
- **Greek:** *eukleia tēs pisteōs autou* — noble renown/fame of/through his faith
- **Ruling:** SOPHIA uses "won noble renown through his faith." "Renown" better captures *eukleia* (good report, glory of reputation) than either "fame" or "glory."

---

## Disagreement 12 — 5:7 "extreme limit of the West" vs. "farthest limit" vs. "farthest edge"

- **EMET:** "extreme limit of the West"
- **LOGOS:** "farthest limit of the West"
- **PNEUMA:** "farthest edge of the West"
- **Greek:** *to terma tēs duseōs* — the boundary/end of the West
- **Ruling:** SOPHIA uses "the extreme limit of the West" (EMET). "Extreme" preserves the sense of an absolute boundary; *terma* = terminus, goal-post, the end of a race-course.

---

## Disagreement 13 — 5:7 "before the rulers" vs. "before rulers" vs. "before emperors and rulers"

- **EMET:** "having borne testimony before the rulers"
- **LOGOS:** "having given his testimony before rulers"
- **PNEUMA:** "gave his testimony before emperors and rulers"
- **Greek:** *martyrēsas epi tōn hēgoumenōn* — having witnessed before the leaders/rulers
- **Ruling:** SOPHIA uses "having given his testimony before rulers." PNEUMA's addition of "emperors" is interpretive (though plausible — Nero); it goes beyond the Greek.

---

## Disagreement 14 — 5:7 "set free from the world" vs. "departed from the world" vs. "departed this world"

- **EMET:** "was set free from the world"
- **LOGOS:** "departed from the world"
- **PNEUMA:** "departed this world"
- **Greek:** *apeluthē tou kosmou* — was released/freed from the world
- **Ruling:** SOPHIA uses "was set free from the world" (EMET). The passive "was set free" suggests divine action, which is appropriate.

---

## Disagreement 15 — 5:7 "greatest example" vs. "most outstanding pattern" vs. "supreme example"

- **EMET:** "greatest example of patient endurance"
- **LOGOS:** "most outstanding pattern of endurance"
- **PNEUMA:** "supreme example of patient endurance"
- **Greek:** *hupomenē hupodigma megiston* — a very great/greatest example of endurance
- **Ruling:** SOPHIA uses "greatest example of patient endurance" (EMET). *Megiston* = greatest; PNEUMA's "supreme" is synonymous but EMET is more literal.

---

*End of disagreement log for 1 Clement Chapter 5. This chapter, containing the earliest non-NT martyrdom accounts of Peter and Paul, required the most careful terminological decisions of any chapter so far.*
